title: Anticipating conflict as large mammals return to Europe's changing countryside

Abstract

Research Highlight: Bluhm, H., Kowalczyk, R., Klich, D., Olech, W., Perzanowski, K., Retez, G., Skorupski, J., Zurell, D., Tracz, M., Tracz, M., Baryło, R., Wołoszyn-Gałęza, A., Januszczak, M., & Kuemmerle, T. (2026). Using individual-based modelling to anticipate future conflict potential for expanding European bison populations. Journal of Applied Ecology, 63(7), e70481. https://doi.org/10.1111/1365-2664.70481. Rural depopulation, legal protection and reintroduction have driven large mammal recovery in parts of Europe; however, escalating human–wildlife conflict constrains the extent of this recovery. Bluhm et al. integrated spatial indicators of crop damage, forestry damage and traffic collisions into an individual-based population model to anticipate where conflict involving European bison (Bison bonasus) may arise over the next century across five Central European countries. The model projected a threefold increase in the bison population to 7580 individuals and continued range expansion. Conflict hotspots emerged in north-eastern Poland (crop damage), western Poland (all conflict types) and western Germany (traffic). The study also identified three low-conflict ‘coldspots’, unlikely to be colonised naturally, as candidate reintroduction sites. Regulating populations at low-conflict densities reduced projected abundance by more than 35% and patch occupancy by nearly 50% over 100 years, whereas increased traffic mortality reduced abundance by approximately 10%. These results expose a trade-off between reducing conflict and restoring the ecological functions of recovering megaherbivores. They favour protecting bison during recovery and deploying non-lethal mitigation in predicted hotspots, and they point to the need for models that capture changing land use and social attitudes.
